laser-001.question: Which correctly describes the photon emitted by stimulated emission?
choices: It has the same frequency as the incident photon, but its direction and phase are random
The incident photon becomes two photons, each with half its energy
It has the same frequency, phase, direction and polarization as the incident photon
laser-001.explanation: When a photon whose energy equals the energy difference between two levels meets an atom in the upper level, it prompts the atom to drop to the lower level and emit a photon in exactly the same state as the incident one — same frequency, phase, direction and polarization. This is stimulated emission: the incident light is amplified with its properties unchanged, which is the origin of the monochromaticity, directionality and coherence of laser light. Random direction and phase are properties of spontaneous emission, which dominates the light from an LED. Splitting into two photons with half the energy each is parametric down-conversion in nonlinear optics, a different phenomenon from stimulated emission.

laser-002.question: For a transition at 1064 nm (photon energy about 1.17 eV), which value is closest to the ratio N₂/N₁ of atoms in the upper and lower levels in thermal equilibrium at 300 K? (Ignore degeneracy and take kT ≈ 0.0259 eV.)
choices: About 1 (roughly equal numbers above and below)
laser-002.explanation: In thermal equilibrium the Boltzmann distribution gives N₂/N₁ = exp(−ΔE/kT). Since ΔE/kT = 1.17 / 0.0259 ≈ 45, N₂/N₁ ≈ e⁻⁴⁵ ≈ 2.4×10⁻²⁰: there are almost no atoms in the upper level. About 1 is the limit at very high temperature (kT ≫ ΔE), which thermal equilibrium can only approach; it does not hold for visible or near-infrared transitions at room temperature. About 10⁻² is a miscalculation of the exponential. In thermal equilibrium N₂ < N₁ always, so light is absorbed and attenuated. Laser oscillation requires artificially creating a population inversion, N₂ > N₁, by pumping from outside.

laser-003.question: Why can a steady-state population inversion (N₂ > N₁) not be obtained in a pure two-level system, even when it is excited with intense light?
choices: Because absorption and stimulated emission occur with equal probability, so even strong pumping only brings the populations toward N₂ = N₁
Because spontaneous emission does not occur in a two-level system, so excited atoms pile up without emitting and no light for lasing is obtained
Because the upper level of a two-level system has an infinitely long lifetime, so atoms once excited never return to the lower level
laser-003.explanation: In a two-level system, the pump light drives upward absorption and downward stimulated emission with the same probability (Einstein coefficients B₁₂ = B₂₁, no degeneracy). However hard you pump, net absorption stops once the populations are equal (absorption saturation), and inversion is never reached. That is why three- and four-level systems are used, in which pumping goes to a separate higher level that relaxes quickly to the upper laser level. Spontaneous emission does occur in a two-level system, and the upper level does not have an infinite lifetime. Semiconductor lasers create the inversion by current injection rather than light.

laser-004.question: Why do four-level lasers such as Nd:YAG reach a lower lasing threshold more easily than three-level lasers such as ruby?
choices: Because in a four-level system the lower laser level is the ground state, so there is no need to excite more than half the atoms
Because the lower laser level lies above the ground state and empties quickly, so even slight pumping creates a population inversion
Because stimulated emission does not occur in a four-level system, so losses are small
laser-004.explanation: In a three-level system (ruby), the lower level of the laser transition is the ground state itself, so creating an inversion requires pumping more than half the ground-state atoms, which makes the threshold high. In a four-level system (Nd:YAG), the lower level lies above the ground state, and atoms that fall into it relax quickly to the ground state, so it stays nearly empty. An inversion therefore exists as soon as there are even a few atoms in the upper level. The option saying “the lower laser level is the ground state” describes a three-level system, the opposite of a four-level one. Stimulated emission is the laser action itself in a four-level system too; without it there would be no lasing.

laser-005.question: An optical resonator is made with two concave mirrors, each with a radius of curvature of 1 m. Which range of mirror spacing L makes the resonator stable (0 ≤ g₁g₂ ≤ 1 with g = 1 − L/R)?
laser-005.explanation: For a symmetric resonator, g₁ = g₂ = 1 − L/R, so g₁g₂ = (1 − L)² (with L in meters). This is at most 1 for 0 ≤ L ≤ 2 m; the end points L = 0 (nearly planar) and L = 2R (concentric resonator) are the stability boundaries. For example, at L = 1.5 m, g = −0.5 and g₁g₂ = 0.25, which is stable, but at L = 2.5 m, g₁g₂ = 2.25, an unstable resonator in which rays move farther from the axis on each round trip. “0 < L < 1 m” mistakes L = R (the confocal resonator) for the upper limit, and “1 m < L < 2 m” misses the lower half. The confocal arrangement has the lowest diffraction loss but is sensitive to mirror misalignment.

laser-006.question: Which value is closest to the longitudinal mode spacing in wavelength of a Fabry–Perot semiconductor laser (wavelength 1550 nm) that is 300 µm long with a group index of 3.6? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
laser-006.explanation: The longitudinal mode spacing in frequency is Δν = c/(2n_gL) = 3.0×10⁸ / (2 × 3.6 × 300×10⁻⁶) ≈ 139 GHz. In wavelength, Δλ = λ²Δν/c = (1550×10⁻⁹)² × 139×10⁹ / 3.0×10⁸ ≈ 1.1 nm. About 2.2 nm ignores the round trip and uses c/(n_gL); about 4.0 nm takes the group index as 1. Because the gain bandwidth spans tens of nanometers, many longitudinal modes tend to lase at once in this type of laser, and in long-distance communication chromatic dispersion distorts the waveform. DFB and DBR lasers use a grating to select a single mode.

laser-007.question: Which value is closest to the Rayleigh range zR of a Gaussian beam with a wavelength of 1064 nm and a beam waist radius w₀ = 0.5 mm?
laser-007.explanation: The Rayleigh range is zR = πw₀²/λ = π × (0.5×10⁻³)² / (1064×10⁻⁹) ≈ 0.74 m. At a distance zR from the waist the beam radius has grown by √2 (the cross-sectional area has doubled), and the range ±zR is where the beam can be regarded as nearly collimated (the confocal parameter, 2zR). About 0.24 m forgets to multiply by π, and about 74 mm is an order-of-magnitude error in unit conversion. Because zR is proportional to w₀ squared, halving the waist cuts the Rayleigh range to 1/4. This is why the depth of focus becomes sharply shallower when a smaller spot is used in laser machining.

laser-008.question: Which value is closest to the far-field half-angle divergence θ of a Gaussian beam (M² = 1) with a wavelength of 1064 nm and a beam waist radius w₀ = 0.5 mm?
laser-008.explanation: The far-field half-angle divergence of a Gaussian beam is θ = λ/(πw₀) = 1064×10⁻⁹ / (π × 0.5×10⁻³) ≈ 6.8×10⁻⁴ rad, or about 0.68 mrad. It can also be written with the Rayleigh range as θ = w₀/zR. About 2.1 mrad is λ/w₀ without dividing by π, and about 0.34 mrad halves the value by confusing the full angle with the half-angle (the full angle is 2θ, about 1.4 mrad). The product of waist radius and divergence, w₀θ = λ/π, is constant, so a narrower beam spreads more. This is the benchmark for beam quality; for real beams the product is M² times larger.

laser-009.question: A 1.064 µm beam (radius w = 5 mm, a nearly collimated Gaussian beam) is focused by a lens with a focal length of 100 mm. Which value is closest to the beam waist radius at the focus? (w₀' ≈ λf/(πw), no aberrations.)
laser-009.explanation: When a nearly collimated Gaussian beam is focused by a lens of focal length f, the waist radius is w₀' ≈ λf/(πw) = 1.064×10⁻⁶ × 0.1 / (π × 5×10⁻³) ≈ 6.8×10⁻⁶ m, or about 6.8 µm (about 14 µm in diameter). About 21 µm forgets to divide by π, and about 0.68 µm is an order-of-magnitude error. The basic ways to shrink the spot are to shorten the focal length or to enlarge the input beam (with a beam expander). However, the smaller the spot, the shallower the depth of focus (2zR = 2πw₀'²/λ), which here is about 0.27 mm. For a beam with M² greater than 1, the spot radius grows by that factor too.

laser-010.question: Which correctly describes a Gaussian beam at a distance of one Rayleigh range zR from its waist?
choices: The beam radius is twice the waist, and the wavefront is flat
The beam radius is √2 times the waist, and the wavefront radius of curvature is at its minimum, 2zR
The beam radius equals the waist, and the wavefront radius of curvature is infinite
laser-010.explanation: The radius of a Gaussian beam is w(z) = w₀√(1 + (z/zR)²), so at z = zR it is √2 w₀. The wavefront radius of curvature is R(z) = z(1 + (zR/z)²): infinite (a flat wavefront) at the waist (z = 0), approaching z far away, and at its minimum value of 2zR at z = zR. The beam radius doubles at z = √3 zR, and the wavefront is not flat there either. The radius equal to the waist with a flat wavefront describes the position z = 0. In addition, the beam picks up an extra phase of π as it passes through the waist (the Gouy phase), which sets the frequencies of a resonator's transverse modes.

laser-011.question: A single-mode fiber laser with M² (beam quality factor) of 1.1 and a multimode laser with M² of 11 (same beam diameter and wavelength) are focused with the same lens. Which correctly gives the ratio of their focused spot radii?
choices: The multimode spot is about 10 times larger
The multimode spot is about 100 times larger
M² affects only the divergence, so both spots are the same size
laser-011.explanation: For a real beam, the product of waist radius and divergence (the beam parameter product, BPP) is M² times that of an ideal Gaussian beam: BPP = M²λ/π. When beams of the same diameter are focused with the same lens, the spot radius is w₀' ≈ M²λf/(πw), proportional to M², so the ratio is 11/1.1 = 10. About 100 times confuses this with the ratio of spot areas (M² squared); the power per unit area (intensity) is about 1/100. M² sets both the divergence and the spot size at once, not just one of them. Compared at the same spot size, the depth of focus is also shallower in inverse proportion to M².

laser-012.question: Which correctly pairs Q-switching and mode locking with their typical pulse durations?
choices: Q-switching gives femtoseconds, mode locking gives milliseconds
Both give microseconds; only the repetition rate differs
Q-switching gives nanoseconds, mode locking gives picoseconds to femtoseconds
laser-012.explanation: Q-switching pumps the gain medium while the resonator loss is held high, storing energy, then suddenly lowers the loss to release it all at once. The pulse duration is a few resonator round-trip times, typically a few to a few tens of nanoseconds. Mode locking fixes the phases of many longitudinal modes so that they interfere to form a single short pulse circulating in the resonator; the wider the gain bandwidth, the shorter the pulse, reaching picoseconds to femtoseconds (around 10 fs is possible with Ti:sapphire). There is no femtosecond Q-switching or millisecond mode locking. Microseconds for both is closer to the time scale of free-running lamp-pumped operation.

laser-013.question: Which value is closest to the pulse repetition rate of a mode-locked laser with a 1.5 m resonator (a linear resonator in air)? (c = 3.0×10⁸ m/s)
laser-013.explanation: In a mode-locked laser, a single pulse circulates in the resonator, and part of it is extracted each time it reaches the output mirror. The repetition rate is the reciprocal of the round-trip time: f = c/(2L) = 3.0×10⁸ / (2 × 1.5) = 1.0×10⁸ Hz, or about 100 MHz. This also equals the longitudinal mode spacing. About 200 MHz divides by the one-way time, and about 50 MHz counts the round trip twice. To raise the repetition rate, shorten the resonator or use harmonic mode locking, which puts several pulses into one round trip. The longitudinal modes of a mode-locked laser form an evenly spaced “optical frequency comb”, which is also used for precision frequency measurement.

laser-014.question: Which value is closest to the spectral width of a transform-limited Gaussian pulse with a center wavelength of 800 nm and a duration (FWHM) of 100 fs? (Time-bandwidth product ΔνΔt = 0.441.)
laser-014.explanation: The frequency width is Δν = 0.441 / Δt = 0.441 / (100×10⁻¹⁵) ≈ 4.4 THz. In wavelength, Δλ = λ²Δν/c = (800×10⁻⁹)² × 4.4×10¹² / 3.0×10⁸ ≈ 9.4 nm. About 0.94 nm and about 94 nm are order-of-magnitude errors. Because of the time-frequency uncertainty relation, shorter pulses need wider spectra; a 10 fs pulse needs roughly 94 nm. If the measured product exceeds 0.441, the pulse is chirped (its frequency changes in time), which indicates room to shorten it further by compensating dispersion with a prism pair or chirped mirrors.

laser-015.question: What is the main reason fiber lasers can maintain good beam quality (M²) even at high power?
choices: Because stimulated emission does not occur in fiber, and only spontaneously emitted light is guided along the core and comes out, so the beam is not disturbed
Because the transverse mode is set by the guiding structure of a single-mode core, and the long, thin shape dissipates heat well and resists thermal lensing
Because over the long fiber the light shifts to a shorter wavelength with less diffraction spreading, which improves the beam quality
laser-015.explanation: In a fiber laser, the core that serves as the gain medium is itself a waveguide, so the transverse mode of the output beam is set by the core's index profile; with a single-mode core, M² is close to 1. Its cross section is also tiny relative to its length, giving a large surface area for cooling, so thermal lensing (index changes from temperature gradients), a problem in solid-state laser rods, barely disturbs the beam. Being a laser, it amplifies light by stimulated emission; spontaneous emission alone cannot give high-power coherent light. The wavelength is set by the rare-earth transition (about 1.03–1.08 µm for ytterbium) and does not get shorter during propagation. The limits to higher power are nonlinear effects such as stimulated Raman scattering, and mode instability.
